candidate.answerReason: If P is the requested product, composing the given power equations gives 4^P=128. Hence 2^(2P)=2^7 and P=7/2.

methods.label: Chain the power equations
methods.explanation:
Each equation begins with the number produced by the preceding equation. Raising one equation to the next exponent therefore lets us combine consecutive exponents into a product. For example,
\[
4^{x_1x_2}=(4^{x_1})^{x_2}=5^{x_2}=6.
\]
All bases are positive, so the power-of-a-power rule applies to these real exponents. Continuing through all 124 equations gives
\[
4^{x_1x_2\cdots x_{124}}=128.
\]
Let \(P=x_1x_2\cdots x_{124}\). Since \(4=2^2\) and \(128=2^7\), this becomes
\[
2^{2P}=2^7.
\]
The function \(2^t\) is strictly increasing, so equal powers have equal exponents. Thus \(2P=7\), giving \(\boxed{\frac72}\), choice D.
methods.levelReason: This route uses positive-base real exponent laws and the injectivity of an exponential function, both standard high-school material.

methods.label: Expose cancellation with logarithms
methods.explanation:
A logarithm records the exponent needed to turn one positive base into another number. For \(j=1,2,\ldots,124\), the given equation therefore says
\[
x_j=\log_{j+3}(j+4).
\]
Changing every logarithm to base \(2\) reveals matching factors:
\[
x_j=\frac{\log_2(j+4)}{\log_2(j+3)}.
\]
Every denominator is nonzero because \(j+3\ge4\), whereas \(2^0=1\). Multiplying gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_1x_2\cdots x_{124}
&=\frac{\log_2 5}{\log_2 4}
  \frac{\log_2 6}{\log_2 5}
  \cdots
  \frac{\log_2 128}{\log_2 127}\\
&=\frac{\log_2 128}{\log_2 4}
=\frac72.
\end{aligned}
\]
Every intermediate logarithm cancels, leaving only the two endpoints. The answer is \(\boxed{\frac72}\), choice D.
methods.levelReason: This is a different standard high-school path at the same AMC 12 level, using logarithm definitions, change of base, and finite cancellation.
